utterances.text: On the 6th of December, you can see the deployment from Ston, the front units of the 2nd Corps, and then on towards Neretva and Mostar. Those were the front-end units of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving down perhaps toward the Dubrovnik area, can you indicate what territory in the Dubrovnik area was held by the 2nd Operational Group as of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the immediate blockade of Dubrovnik, you can see units of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, you can see units of the Territorial Defence from the Trebinje Battalion, and the Trebinje TO detachment. You can also see the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade immediately surrounding the town. These were the basic units that we used -- or rather, positioned around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think at this point, Mr. Usher, we can go ahead and put it on the ELMO. The emphasis will be on the Dubrovnik area and the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd, if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can I just ask you whether or not the naval situation, so we can discuss the waters first, had changed as of the 6th of December from your previous indications on the earlier map.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation on the sea remained the same. You can see a symbolic presence of boats along the patrol lines blocking the town in the Mljet channel, just off the coast of Dubrovnik itself and in front of Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you perhaps adjust the map so that more of the area of the 3rd of the 472nd is centred and covered. Yeah. Even a bit more to the left, please. Thank you very much. Okay. Good. And focusing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you discuss, please, the positions of the companies of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade that are in position -- that are visible on the map. And if you could take your pointer and just show the territory that the 3rd Battalion had occupied as of that date, as of the 2nd -- I'm sorry, actually as of the 5th, the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the combat deployment of the units of the 3rd Battalion if you go from the right flank. You can see in the area of the Strincijera fort, the 3rd Company of that battalion. In the central area of this combat deployment, you can see the 2nd Company in the Bosanka area. Along the left flank in the Zarkovica area, you can see the 1st Company of the 3rd Battalion. You can see the battalion's command post at Brgat, and an observation post at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you just assist us before going on about the distance between these areas you've just talked about and the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Strincijera fort to the Old Town, the distance is about 3 kilometres. Between Bosanka and the Old Town, less than 2 kilometres. And finally, between Zarkovica and the Old Town, about 2 and a half kilometres. As the crow flies, all of these distances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at these three positions you've just discussed, can you describe -- I'm sorry, four positions, can you describe the weapons that were situated at each position, and if you could indicate the name of the position and then the weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Strincijera fort, there were infantry elements with simple weapons. I think they had four 82-millimetre mortars. The range is about 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. What unit is that that you're referring to at Strincijera? What unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the 3rd Company of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You just indicated that the range was about 2 kilometres. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does that range bring those weapons within firing distance of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some sections of the Old Town, maybe half the Old Town. Yes, it would have been in effective firing range.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Company, in the Bosanka area, had the same kind of weapons, but they also had several 20-millimetre guns and there were two tanks in the area for support in the operations that the company was carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were the 80 -- I'm sorry, were the weapons within firing range of the Old Town in the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Zarkovica area there was an anti-armour company, which had weapons for direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you please point out Zarkovica, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And which weapons for direct fire did that company have? What type of direct fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had four recoilless guns, 82 millimetre was the calibre. Four 82-millimetre mortars. It had two 20-millimetre guns, too. And it also had three launchers, the Maljutkas; anti-armour missiles, wire-guided.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain the Maljutka as a weapon. Can you explain a little bit about its operation. If you say "wire-guided," it is a direct fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an anti-armour missile used for the destruction of armoured targets, usually tanks, forts, ramparts, strongly fortified targets. It is wire guided. The crew handling the weapon must have the target in sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you again, please, with your pointer point out Zarkovica so that we make sure we're pointing to the same ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There. Thank you very much. I think you just showed Bosanka. Could you please identify Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the place with symbol for the anti-armour weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the observation post of the battalion commander was also here, the observation post from which he observed the areas in which his companies were deployed as well as the axis of their attack. My apologies, I pointed out Bosanka, yes, you're quite right, where the black ellipse is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the particular battalion commander you're referring to is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this is the same map, the positions are the same as they would have been on the 6th of December with these particular weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back for a minute to the 1st Company. I believe it's -- the focus is not terribly good, so I don't know if there's a way to -- it looks like it's at Bosanka. Can you discuss, please -- thanks, that's much better. Please discuss what weapons were available at that position and whether they were in range of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Bosanka there was the 1st Company. A while ago I made a slight mistake. It had the same composition as the 2nd and 3rd Companies, however the anti-armour company in the black ellipse is not marked by a number, so that's why I made the mistake. This anti-armour company that had the missiles and other weapons. All these companies had the same composition in terms of the weapons they had. They had 82-millimetre launchers, but the central one at Bosanka also had two tanks in addition as support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is the position at Zarkovica - just going back for a moment - in the direct line of fire to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm corrected to say line of observation. Is it the direct line of observation to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, are you able to indicate if all four units of the 3rd Battalion were within firing range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can we take a look now at the other positions that are in the Dubrovnik area that are indicated on this map. If you could slide the map a little bit perhaps to your left, maybe up and to the left. To the left. Thank you. And up a bit, please. We want to show the term "9th VPS" and the position there, if it's easily visible. You were fine. That's good. Fine. Thank you. Okay. Can you identify, please, the positions that are shown here, including whatever is marked as 9 VPS, what it represents, and just tell us as quickly as you can about the positions, location, identification. What does the flag 9 VPS in that red circle indicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th VPS marks the command that is in charge of all these units marked on the map. The small flag --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I want to know. Tell me, please, what the flag which is at a location in a circle, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies. In Kupari, there was the forward observation post of the 9th VPS. The command post is located at Kupari, within this circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Moving perhaps up a little bit -- let's see if we can get the usher to assist us there. Okay. Thank you. Can you indicate, there are some abbreviations, "OdTO-Tr." It's slightly larger than the other print. "OdTO-Tr." No, it's a bit -- centre it a bit. If you come down a bit, please. "OdTO-Tr.," what does that stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This writing stands for the abbreviation Territorial Defence Detachment Trebinje. This is a battalion-level unit; it's a bit weaker than a battalion would normally be, subordinated to the 9th Sector when the brigade was pulled out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And there are some indications -- symbols there. One is a black circle with a red symbol inside, if you can see it. If you move down a little bit. Come back, down, please. Down again. In that area, the black circle with the red indication -- yeah, that one. Yes, what does that stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the mortar platoon. They had 82-millimetre mortars. It's a mortar unit belonging to that battalion. The battalion was not very strong in terms of artillery. This mortar unit was all they had. The position of that platoon is given here as well as the command post of the Territorial Defence unit where the flag is. You can see a red circle just next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, was that position, the one in the circle -- no, the next -- with the black circle and the red marking, was that -- keep going -- yeah, yes. Was that in firing range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This unit was not trained on the Old Town. Its axis of operation was down towards Rijeka Dubrovacka. The front ends of that unit are here, of that detachment. This platoon acts as support for that unit along the axis of attack, but it's not within firing range of the town, nor is it along the same axis of that detachment of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where you have your pointer right now, if you could move up to the area where it says "BVG/3mtb." Could you discuss those positions and what the symbols mean, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a firing group belonging to the battalion. That is only its short name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of what battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 3rd Battalion. This is a battalion firing group of the 3rd Battalion providing support for other units of the 3rd Battalion. It's a 120-millimetre mortar battery containing six mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was -- were the weapons that you've just discussed in range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From that position, it was possible to target the Old Town. The range is 6 kilometres, and the distance is between 5 and 6 kilometres. That's at the edge of the firing range, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what is the name of the area where those weapons were found, where those positions were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uskoplje, the railway station of Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you could indicate what the "mpoad" stands for. It's just to the left of your pointer right now. "Mpoad," what does that stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stands for Mixed Anti-armour Artillery Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where is that as well? Where is its location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That division -- well, in fact, it wasn't the entire division that was there. There were anti-armour guns ZIS, 76-millimetre, but this marking is wrong. Not the entire division was there, only those four guns were actually there. I do happen to know this for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that attached to which battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. They got this from their brigade as support, as a kind of reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you -- can you discuss the weapons that were part of that, that were available.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the anti-armour guns, ZIS 76-millimetres. The range was about 4 kilometres. This is only a symbol, but the positions of those guns were in a different place. All in all, this was given only because the firing group was within that unit. But these positions given here are not their exact positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have "bTO-Tr." where your pointer is now. What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebinje Territorial Defence Battalion. That's what it means. This is their command post, and the units are to the right. You can see their combat disposition here. These are the units that are part of that combat disposition, and this here means that the command of that battalion was located right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What weapons were available to those units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This TO unit was poorly armed, and the battalion was usually deployed along the auxiliary axis, where there weren't many operations underway. They only had the 82-millimetre launchers, same as the Territorial Defence detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were those weapons within range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you can move perhaps the map a little bit to cover the bigger encircled area -- yeah. That's it. That's good. Can you start at the top and indicate what -- we're in a circle now where the unit that we're talking about says "3/5 pmtbr." What does that mean? It says "3/5 pmtbr." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 3rd Battalion of the 5th pmtbr. Well, it's the Proletarian Motorised Brigade. That was the official name of that unit. The last map, there was something that I couldn't figure out, those units and those abbreviations. I think those referred to this unit, "pmtbr," Proletarian Motorised Brigade, I think that's what the abbreviation actually stands for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, to whom was that unit subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're saying the 9th Naval Sector, your sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was that part of the 2nd Operational Group on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can we look now at the markings. Starting at the centre, there's a flag.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the command post of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is the location of the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Podbrijezje. That's where it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking above, where it says "BVG-3," what is that position and what is its location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the battalion firing group equivalent to the kind of weapons that the 3rd Battalion had, 120-millimetre mortars, and it is the area above Mocinska Spilja. There is a graveyard there and the firing position was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were they within range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking up above - above - there's a red circle, a bigger red circle. Do you see it? Yeah. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a rear unit, "poz."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of what formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the logistics unit of the battalion. Each battalion has a logistics unit for supplies, ammunition, and all the other supplies. It's actually a platoon that's used for the purpose -- a bit less than a platoon, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. So that belongs to the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We would like to take a look now, if you could raise the map a little bit, please. Sorry, no. If you can bring it so we have a closer look at the various subunits. That's it. Okay. Looking over to the section of the 3rd of the 5th, look at 1/3. What does that represent? Mm-hmm. That's it. What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the 1st Company of that battalion. The combat disposition is along the coast.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where is that? Can you give us a location indication, please, for that company.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's at Zaton.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what weaponry was there on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Small arms with small mortars, 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And what range -- were they within range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to the centre -- yeah. 2 -- 2nd Company of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is that located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the area can be seen left of Mokosica, Podbrijezje. The broader area of the village of Podbrijezje. They have the same weapons like the previous, 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what is the range of those weapons? Is it -- are those weapons within range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Company was somewhat removed towards the back, and they had the same weapons like the previous two ones did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And were they also -- were they in range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, there's a symbol of a -- with a flag, and it -- the symbol is to the right of the word "Mokosica," if you see it. Can you tell us what that represents, please. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the command of the settlement of Mokosica. It's a rather big settlement and all the surrounding settlements belong to it. The command of this settlement is responsible for law and order and the proper functioning of these settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are some broken lines within this circle, broken red lines. Do you see them? Yeah. Within the circle and generally around. What do those signify, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front end positions of this battalion of the Territorial Defence of Trebinje. These are its companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we ask you to move the map so that Cilipi is shown. Are you able to point out, please - yeah - the area of Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The airport of Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there -- first of all, under -- to whom were units there subordinated and what units were there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battery, the mobile battery, of 130-millimetre cannons was there. Its position can be seen at the end of the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And to whom -- well, what unit was actually there? Name the unit, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobile battery of 130-millimetre cannons, and it was subordinated to the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So those were sector weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were those weapons within firing range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Almost as far as they could be, but they could be targeted. The distance was about 12 or 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what is the range of a 130-millimetre cannon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 kilometres. That is the effective range, and its ultimate range is over 20 kilometres; 24 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at a flag that's -- that appears on the map, can you see it? It -- a red symbol with a flag on it near -- it says near Cavtat. What is that, please? The flag, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the command post of Cavtat, in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the command post for what formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a newly established command post. It doesn't have a formation. This is a small unit for providing security so that life itself could function. How can I explain this? So the traffic would evolve, so that looting would be prevented, everything that is needed in that kind of situation. All such things were to be resolved by this command, a few officers and a few men. It was not intended for combat use.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there any heavy weapons in that location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you where the command post of the 2nd Operational Group is on this map. I think you may have to move it to show us, but if you could do that. Yeah. In this small red circle in the town of Trebinje, it says on the flag, the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the area is called?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could move the map back for a moment to show the area of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can you indicate, in addition to the heavy weaponry that you discussed earlier, were there also rifles or sniper rifles available to all units in this area? "Sniping equipment" perhaps is a more technical term.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, there were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the 3rd Battalion then had sniping equipment, as a follow-on to this? The 3rd of the 472nd had sniping equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this equipment was usable within range of the Old Town -- do you know -- was it subject to being used generally during the course of the Dubrovnik operations period? Were they weapons used?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards to the 3rd Battalion, I don't think so. I think the answer is no. Because at that time, it did not have sniper weapons of that range and they didn't need it either. They had enough machine-guns, submachine-guns, and other automatic weapons, so they didn't really need this sniping equipment. I think that, according to establishment, they only had one or two sniper shooters, but with ordinary sniper rifles, with a short range, a kilometre or something. They didn't have special snipers with a longer range.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you repeat again the distance between Zarkovica and Srdj, just remind us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Zarkovica and Srdj, there is approximately 1 kilometre -- perhaps a kilometre and 200 metres, perhaps a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the positions you have taken us to and shown, would you conclude that it is only the units of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade that had firing range of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you just give us an idea of if there was any change in the coastal situation, the waters -- the water patrols on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, these ships were not firing. What is drawn on this map are symbolically depicted areas of patrolling, but that does not mean that the boats were in those positions actually on the 6th of December. Perhaps one boat was here, perhaps way up here on the 6th of December. So these are not the positions of the ships at that time. This is only a symbolical depiction as to what the boats are doing, if there are three of them, and where their positions usually where. On the 6th of December, they were not operating from there because they did not receive such orders and no operations on their part were planned for the 6th of December. Also, there were no plans for the 3rd Battalion either, because there was a cease-fire in force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was my next series of questions, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we could remove the map and move it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P132.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you have indicated that this map, which is dated the 2nd of December but is equally valid as for positions as of the 6th of December, on this map there are considerable heavy weapons remaining in the area of Dubrovnik. Was there an operation, a combat operation, planned for the time frame of up to this -- between the 2nd and the 6th of December in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No operations were planned between the 2nd and the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a military necessity on the 6th of December to have these positions so close to the Old Town within firing range of the heavy weaponry of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such military necessity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of comprehensive cease-fire negotiations that were undertaken in connection with a resolution to the situation in Dubrovnik between the JNA and members of the -- of a Dubrovnik negotiating team about the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was given the task of leading these negotiations on the 5th of December in Cavtat, in the morning, together with the negotiating team of the Croatian side. On the Croatian side there were three ministers; Rudolf Davorin, Cifric, and Kriste.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what other persons were on your negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence officer of my command was with me, Captain Jeremic, Sofronije Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the intention behind the negotiations? What was to be achieved? What were some of the terms that were on the table?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the final negotiations regarding a settlement to the problem of Dubrovnik, or this crisis around Dubrovnik, aimed at normalising life in Dubrovnik. Those 11 points were given up on, or part of them, rather, the ones that had been discussed earlier. Practically on the 3rd of December, General Strugar conveyed to me, after he was in Belgrade, that I was supposed to lead these negotiations on the 5th of December, together with the ministers that I referred to already. It was said that various requests should be given up on, namely to surrender arms, and to hand over volunteers, or rather, to revert to the previous situation regarding MUP personnel levels in Dubrovnik. So these requests that were within those 11 points were given up on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "MUP personnel," could you please identify what "MUP" means. I know it's an abbreviation, but if you could tell us what's referred to.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, which grew through mobilisation in Dubrovnik. So the intention was to reduce the number of their members.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any meeting or briefing involving JNA commanding officers on the 3rd of December that you might be able to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that on that day there was a meeting at the General Staff, at the Supreme Command, and the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar, took part in this as did Admiral Kandic, commander of the navy, as well as other army commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you take part as well? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was not my level. I was not at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who actually led these negotiations? Who spoke? Who was the -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. Who chaired this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the meeting was chaired by General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... where?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general staff, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What, if any, orders did General Adzic convey to those commanders present? Do you know? Did you find out what the items in the meeting covered?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of the agenda. I don't know what the substance of that meeting was, but I know what the orders were, what General Adzic ordered General Strugar to convey. And General Strugar asked Admiral Kandic to convey this to me in Kumbor in relation to these negotiations. I think it was decided at that meeting that final negotiations should be held with Croatia regarding the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia and the acceptance of the Vance plan. I don't know the details. I just know what I was told in terms of what I was supposed to do about Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain or do you know why Admiral Kandic was asked to relay these points to you, since you were under the 2nd Operational Group? You were subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group, so why would Admiral Kandic have been the messenger?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons. I cannot state any; I can only make assumptions. Admiral Kandic came to Kumbor from Podgorica by helicopter en route to the island of Vis. Since he was going that direction and he reached my area of command, then General Strugar asked him to convey to this to me. I think that General Strugar stayed back in Podgorica or he went to Trebinje, to his command post. I don't know that. He was certainly prevented by some reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, it is, Your Honour. Your Honour, may I, just before we break, indicate to the Chamber, I would ask for a bit more time on Monday to complete the examination-in-chief of Admiral Jokic. There is a bit of material that I think merits the detail that I want to go into and will be helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What does "a bit more time" mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have the other witness lined up, so perhaps -- no more than three hours, perhaps two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that indication. We will take the second break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, returning to the point you were making about the meeting on the 3rd of December, where General Adzic gave certain directions, what did you learn about what was ordered by General Adzic as to placing units within the 2nd Operational Group under control, under total control? What was addressed, if anything, about levels of control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I was told was that full control was to be established over the subordinated units to not respond to any acts of provocation, not to exacerbate tensions with Dubrovnik, and to continue negotiations in a flexible way. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned also that this cease-fire that was on the table was connected with more global issues beyond Dubrovnik. I believe you said about the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. Does that indicate that every area where there was JNA presence had some local level of negotiation? By "local," I mean that cease-fire negotiations had to be conducted in every area of conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe this was only a part of a more comprehensive plan, an all-encompassing plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that it was very important to have this particular Dubrovnik component of the plan work, be effective, be brought into action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the level of negotiator for the Croatian side, I believe you indicated Davorin Rudolf, Mr. Cifric, and Mr. Kriste. Were these local persons from Dubrovnik or what level were they representing in the Croatian structure?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were ministers in the Croatian government. And on their way from Zagreb heading south, they had other problems to deal with south of Split, I believe, on the island of Vis. And their final destination was Dubrovnik. That was the highest negotiation level possible for us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The prior negotiations had been handled on a different level, any other meetings concerning cease-fires in Dubrovnik. I say cease-fires; on what level had those generally been handled?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier talks were between our negotiating team, led by Colonel Svicevic and his deputy, Captain Jeremic, on behalf of the 2nd Operational Group. The opposite side was represented by representatives of the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff and the monitors of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know what General Strugar's attitude was toward the upcoming comprehensive cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the one who conveyed the words of General Adzic to Admiral Kandic and then told Admiral Kandic to tell me, the way I just told you. I think that reflected his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- were you designated by whom -- or by whom were you designated to conduct the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I was told, how I was informed about that, and my understanding was that I was designated on the basis of what General Strugar had told Admiral Kandic. But I did not have any firsthand account of this. This was told to me by Admiral Kandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation with the units in the areas around Dubrovnik? What was the general attitude or morale of those units at that time? When I say "units," I mean the units of the 2nd Operational Group around Dubrovnik. What was the morale like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was understood that the crisis was nearing a settlement. It was peaceful. There were no combat operations and everyone was waiting for this final solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any perceptible sense of frustration about the operation in Dubrovnik from a military perspective of the units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a sense of frustration, especially so with the more extremist elements or individuals who were dissatisfied with the outcome. There was discontent with regard to why the war had been waged in the first place and why people died, but they failed to hand over their weapons and the reservists had not been demilitarised. Certainly some of the senior officers, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how long had some of those units --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a problem with the interpretation. Page 66, line 7: [In English] "... and the reservists had not been demilitarised." [Interpretation] I believe the admiral was talking about the discontent by the reservists, not about them being militarised or demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you like me to clarify that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, there may have been an issue of interpretation. I wonder if you could go back. My question was: "Was there any perceptible sense of frustration about the operation in Dubrovnik from a military perspective of the units." Your answer was not quite clear. I wonder if you could revisit it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, roughly -- I mean, my opinion is as follows: The fighters were dissatisfied, especially some of the more extremist individuals were dissatisfied about the outcome of the operation, because Dubrovnik had not been disarmed and the expectations of the units had not been met. Dubrovnik did not accept any of the terms in terms of the surrender of the volunteers, them leaving town, or the handing over of weapons. Certain individuals questioned the reason for war, why people were killed, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These negotiations which were considered so important were represented or had the Croatian minister level on that side, what was your understanding of why the operational group commander would not have -- was not conducting these negotiations? Why were you designated to do so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to answer that question. Actually, I don't know why I was designated, but I was. It's a fact. I'm not sure what guided them in making that decision. I find it very hard to speculate what the commander of the 2nd Operational Group had in mind when assigning me, or the chief of the General Staff. That's what I was told and that's what I did. I carried out those tasks. I'm afraid I might make a mistake if I were to speculate on the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I checked my transcript and my signal went down. Was it known --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting, Your Honour. What the Admiral said is that he didn't know what guided the commander of the Operational Group or the chief of the General Staff to designate him, which does not exactly follow from page 67, lines 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, that I see a lack of clarity in that. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's just the structure of the sentence, I think. I think it comes through clear enough that both commander of the 2nd Operational Group and the chief of the General Staff had determined to designate Admiral Jokic to this task, which is the point being made by Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then, Admiral, your point is you don't know. You don't know. You don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate generally what General Strugar's attitude towards cease-fire agreements and peace negotiations was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't speculate. I can't second-guess what his attitude may have been. As a soldier at the highest possible level, he carried out his orders, the orders that he received. Now, what his personal opinion was, I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When were cease-fire negotiations set to take place in the Dubrovnik area between the designee of the 2nd Operational Group and the Croatian ministers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were set to begin on the 5th of December, I believe, at about 11.00, in Cavtat. The negotiators had arrived by ship. We secured safe passage for them, and the negotiations were held and were over by 1400 hours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were the negotiations finalised, in other words signed and sealed, or was there at least some understanding that there would be an agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An agreement was reached quite soon. My understanding of the overall tone of the negotiations and the objective was to accept the requests made by Dubrovnik and to give up our own requests in terms of volunteers handing over their weapons. I think effectively the negotiations and dealing with the requests of the Dubrovnik side only took a very short time, and all their requests were accepted fully, with the exception of one point, and that was control of the ships.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, can you discuss, please, what that control of the ships point entailed. What was the actual issue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was only about the way and place where control of the incoming and outgoing ships would take place. Based on the agreement, we agreed for Dubrovnik to be open to incoming ships and traffic from the mainland. The question was: Where will the checks be conducted to keep weapons from being smuggled into Dubrovnik, as well as other combat needs. The ministers wanted these checks to be performed within the town itself. Based on my experience, however, and knowing what the procedure used to be earlier when plenty of ships were entering Dubrovnik, were inspected, and there were a number of incidents related to that, I proposed that the checks be performed on the sea. Bearing in mind the safety of my men in the town itself, which was a hostile environment, this could have given rise to further incidents. So this was the only point of disagreement we had. We agreed for me to check again with my superiors and to sign the agreement the next day. As for all the other points of the agreement, everything else was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was it your perception that both sides, both yourself, both the 2nd Operational Group representatives, and the Croatian side, left the meeting with the same understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What time of day was the meeting to resume the next day for finalisation of the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that I would get back to them about the time, but I believe we agreed on the same time as the day before, 10.00 or 11.00, roughly speaking. That was when the agreement in Cavtat was supposed to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: After these negotiations on the 5th of December, did you report to General Strugar about the meeting, about the terms of the negotiations, about the cease-fire in general, any outstanding issue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once the negotiations were completed, I went to Trebinje and I informed General Strugar at his command post with all the terms and all the modalities of the agreement. I also pointed out that the agreement had not been signed, but that was a merely formal matter. Essentially there were no differences, no discrepancies. The only disagreement was about checking the ships. He did not wish to go about it this way. He believed it was a naval problem in its nature, that it was related to the navy, and he thought that it should have been up to me to decide whether these checks would have been carried out on the sea or in the town itself. He did not wish to go any further into that. As for all the other terms, those were never challenged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated, Admiral, that you had agreed to return around 10.00 or 11.00 the next day. Now, when was the cease-fire, after your return at 10.00 or 11.00, actually, in its entirety, to go into effect? What time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that the agreement was to be signed at about that time, we decided that the cease-fire should take effect at 1200 hours on the 6th of December, in order to comply with its final formal matter in terms of when the cease-fire would begin. Essentially, however, we ordered our units to start the cease-fire in the morning, on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you communicate to your units the fact that a cease-fire and that a significant cease-fire was about to be going into effect? By what means did you issue orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having reported to General Strugar in Trebinje, I returned to my command post in Kupari, where I explained to my staff what the agreement was about as well as the terms of the agreement. And I ordered them to convey to all the units this message about the complete cease-fire that was to begin on the morning of the 6th. Even as early as the 5th, that day, there were no operations, no firing, but formally it was decided that the cease-fire would take place the following morning and all operations would cease, all operations against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you receive an order from General Strugar to cease fire -- excuse me, to put into effect -- to make sure that the cease-fire would be put into effect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Decision on Further Operations, as the combat document is entitled, the 6th of December, at the very end of the document it reads: "The cease-fire shall take effect at 1200 hours on the 6th of December." That's part of his order, and it was even underlined.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the order was complied with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as concerns the other units, with the exception of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Explain, please, what happened with the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade; what and when.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, having carried out that task, I returned, and having in mind the fact that there was to be a cease-fire, I was facing difficulty evacuating units and commands. From the 5th Military Naval Sector of Pula, I went back to Kumbor to my original command post, where I spent the night. The next day, the next morning, I received word from my operations centre. I received a phone call from the duty operations officer, Captain Slobodan Kozaric. At about 4.45 in the morning, just before 5.00 a.m., he reported to me that Captain Kovacevic had got in touch from his command post at Gornji Brgat to say that he was under fire from the Dubrovnik side, especially from the front end of Srdj and that one of his men had been killed and two wounded by that time. He said, "I'm now leaving for my observation post at Zarkovica to see what's going on." Kozaric warned him that I had issued an order, an explicit order, to not go anywhere or attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "the morning of," what date are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Admiral said that Kozaric conveyed to him that Kovacevic had told Kozaric that one of his men had already been killed. This, unfortunately, did not enter the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I see the omission there. It certainly was reported in the English translation as the evidence was given. It was reported by the -- to the Admiral that Captain Kovacevic had indicated that one of his men had been killed. That might be checked in the transcript in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you had just begun to answer my question when counsel needed to have a clarification. When you said "that day," what day were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The same day that the cease-fire we have been discussing was to go into effect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do upon hearing this information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered Kozaric to stop the attack -- or rather, I ordered him first of all to warn Kovacevic that he should not attack and to inform Zec, who was chief of staff, and Colonel Kovacevic, who was supposed to be at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know from where Kozaric telephoned you? Where was he when he telephoned you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He phoned me from the operations centre at the forward command post at Kupari, the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where were you, Admiral? Where did he phone you to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Kumbor, at my original command post. The distance is between 45 and 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did Kozaric tell Captain Kovacevic? I know you've mentioned a Colonel Kovacevic, now I'm talking about Captain Kovacevic. What did Kozaric tell Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cautioned him that there had been an explicit order issued by myself that there were to be no operations, that a cease-fire had taken effect. His answer was: I am now going to the observation post to see what is going on, because I'm not exactly clear about the situation. That was the answer by Captain Kovacevic, and he left the Brgat command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Further to your instructions to Kozaric, who communicated with Captain Kovacevic, what happened afterward?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 6.00, Kozaric called me again, saying that Captain Kovacevic had told him to start the attack on Srdj, because they could no longer cope with this lethal fire. Then again he was warned about the cease-fire and that he shouldn't do it. He said: "I still have time before 12.00, and I may need artillery" -- or he said, "I will need artillery," something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, when you say: "Captain Kovacevic told him to start the attack on Srdj," who is "him"? Who did Captain Kovacevic tell?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the Croatian side, you indicated, was equally in agreement about the cease-fire negotiations. Did your command post contact the Croatian side to find out what was going on, to inquire about the allegations by Captain Kovacevic about activities up -- from the Srdj area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I was concerned and my reaction at the time, I did not bear that in mind. For me, the highest priority was to stop the attack, knowing what an attack on Srdj would have meant. It was perfectly clear to me that attacking Srdj was the same as attacking Dubrovnik, or rather, that firing on the city would follow. That's why I wanted to stop that attack at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To clarify a point, when Captain Kovacevic spoke to your operations officer Kozaric, who did -- who was going to start the attack? Who was actually -- who did Kovacevic mean was going to start an attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant the Srdj feature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, was it Kovacevic who was going to start the attack? Perhaps I wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. After hearing that Captain Kovacevic was going to start the attack, what happened from your own officers? What did you hear next from them? This would be after the phone call from chief of staff Zec.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, I had asked to speak to Captain Kovacevic [as interpreted], and I ordered Kozaric to pass me the commander of the 3rd Battalion so that I could speak to him. He said, however, that Captain Kovacevic had hung up and that he left to go back to his own unit, or that perhaps a shell had interrupted communications and that's why the line broke down. Therefore, I was not able to speak to the commander of the 3rd Battalion. Then I ordered him to let me speak to the chief of staff, Zec. After that, Captain Kozaric informed me that the chief of staff was not at the command post and nor was Captain Kovacevic, who was another person that I asked to speak to. I conveyed to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Colonel Kovacevic, 76, line 1. Not Captain Kovacevic, Colonel Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And after that, what occurred? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we get that clear. We have two Kovacevics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we go back, I'm going to ask you: You asked to speak to Captain Kovacevic and "ordered Kozaric to pass me the commander of the 3rd Battalion so that I could speak to him. He said, however, that Captain Kovacevic had hung up and that he left to go back to his own unit, or perhaps a shell had interrupted communications and that's why the line broke down." And then another sentence: "After that, Captain Kozaric informed me that the chief of staff was not at the command post, nor was Captain Kovacevic, who was another person that I asked to speak to." Did you mean Captain Kovacevic or Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Colonel Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what is the first name? Who is Colonel Kovacevic, if you'd remind us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Kovacevic, Gavrilo Kovacevic, my assistant for the land forces, who was in charge of control and monitoring operations by the 3rd Battalion throughout the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral, for straightening that out. Were you ever able to reach Chief of Staff Zec?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued an order to Captain Kozaric to find for me the chief of staff and Colonel Kovacevic, to find them, to bring them back to the command post, and to -- for the chief of staff to immediately get in touch with me. As time went by, this became an urgent matter. This became a top priority for me to stop the attack by the battalion. But time went by, and at about 7.00 -- it's very difficult for me to say now. It was at about 7.00, give or take a minute or two, I received a call from the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did General Strugar say to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had received a call by I believe General Kadijevic or the chief of the General Staff, it could have been either of those two, and that they asked him about the attack on Dubrovnik, what sort of attack it was, who was carrying out the attack and what the whole situation was about. I was really very surprised. I was stunned. I told him what I had heard, what I had heard from the operations centre, that the commander of the 3rd Battalion was about to launch an attack on Srdj because he could no longer put up with heavy fire, that he was sustaining heavy losses, and so on and so forth. He told me that General Kadijevic was furious, that an agreement had been signed for a cease-fire to take place and how, given that, could a battalion be launching an attack under those circumstances? I told him that I would look into the matter, that I ordered the chief of staff to get back to me, and that I would stop the attack. I don't know if it was already then that he told me - I believe he did - that General Kadijevic had ordered for us as soon as we dealt with the situation to come to Belgrade as soon as possible and that he would be sending a plane over to fetch us for consultations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Given the critical nature of the situation, why did you not contact General Strugar immediately, before he contacted you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not know that the town was being attacked. The attack was limited to Srdj, that is one matter. Secondly, the most urgent thing for me was to resolve this combat situation; namely, to stop the attack and to prevent any damage in town, to prevent losses in the unit, not to inform my superiors. It was more important for me to prevent worse things from happening rather than make telephone calls and lose time, waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What time did the attack start?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack itself, as the battalion commander said, started around 6.00, perhaps a few minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say that: "The most urgent thing for me was to resolve this combat situation; namely, to stop the attack to prevent any damage in town, to prevent losses in the unit," what did you mean? What damage and -- "not to inform my supervisors." Explain, please, what you meant by that. Why would you not inform your head of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean that I was not supposed to inform my superiors; I thought that the priority of my steps, the steps I'm supposed to take was the following: First to stop a worsening, an urgent worsening of the situation. Because I had the picture before my eyes. I knew where the units were, and I knew that it was a question of minutes rather than hours and that the most important thing for me was to stop the attack and to prevent attacks on Srdj, knowing that attacks on Srdj were attacks on town, too. That's the way it was in November. Every shell that missed Srdj hit the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When Captain Kozaric telephoned at 5.45, had the attack started? Could you hear --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness never said that he was informed at 5.45. He said 4.45. The Prosecutor is saying "5.45" without any foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When next you heard from Captain Kozaric about an attack underway -- or that an attack was to be started, could you hear any evidence of an attack in background or could you, from any source, hear evidence of an attack? Do you know if Captain Kozaric may have heard evidence of an attack or shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course I couldn't hear anything, because I was very far away. Kozaric did hear some sounds, but he was not sure at 4.45 who it was and from what side. He could establish that only at 6.00 when he made his second telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you come to learn that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was attacked? At any point in time, did you come to learn that the Old Town of Dubrovnik had been shelled or attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that only later. After having spoken to General Strugar, I received one or two calls from Dubrovnik. The first call was that the Old Town was being shelled. And I said to them that it was impossible, bearing in mind that this was around 8.30 perhaps. I'm not sure of the time now. It was between 8.00 and 9.00. I said that I am trying to establish what the situation was and what was going on, but that I did not believe that the Old Town was being targeted. The subordinate commander said that he was going to attack Srdj. After a certain amount of time - I don't know exactly, the communications were very poor - about half an hour later, the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik called again and on the line was Minister Rudolf Davorin. He said to me: Admiral, this is now indeed an operation against the Old Town. He even turned the receiver that way. And I then had to believe it, because in the meantime I had received information that units were already at Srdj. I said to him that I was very sorry at that moment. If all of this proves to be true, this is an arbitrary attack of a lower-ranking commander. I would stop that attack, I would try to resolve that as soon as possible, because the communication links were broken. He said that an effort should be made to do this straight away. I said I think around 11.00, I think that we are going to resolve the situation by 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you indicated that Minister Rudolf turned the receiver. What did you hear when he turned the receiver of whatever phone he was using?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the sound of shelling. I assumed that -- I mean, I know where the municipality is, the municipality building of Dubrovnik, and that is within the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how General Kadijevic -- sorry. You indicated that -- I believe that General Kadijevic had telephoned from Belgrade, angry. How would he have known about the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I simply could not believe how it was possible for General Kadijevic in Belgrade to know about the attack on town and I did not know about this, and General Strugar, too. And of course this was astonishing to me. And I couldn't figure it out then. However, later I realised, from talking to Minister Rudolf, how this happened. The representative of the European Community - I don't know whether it was Di Mistura - used a satellite telephone to make a call because he could not reach [Realtime transcript read in error "General Strugar"] me or General Strugar. He telephoned Belgrade directly, and that is how Kadijevic found out quite early.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 81, line 12, "and me," the witness said. And here it says only "General Strugar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you confirm that, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, if I can just ask you again. My question was: "Do you know -- I'm sorry. You indicated that I believe General Kadijevic had telephoned from Belgrade, angry. How would he have known about the attack?" Then I'll begin to read back. "At that time, I simply did not believe how it was possible for General Kadijevic in Belgrade to know about the town and I did not know about this. And General Strugar, too. And of course this was astonishing to me." We move on, it says: "The representative -- and I did not know about this and General Strugar, too. Then the representative from the European Community - I don't know whether it was Di Mistura - used a satellite telephone to make a call because he could not reach General Strugar." Then the question was: "Was there anyone else he could not reach?"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They called the command at Kumbor. They called me, too, but they could not reach me. And they had the telephone of General Kadijevic, so they managed to reach him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Was there a system of some sort in place for communications that would have allowed the 2nd Operational Group command to receive information about the attack when it happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the 2nd Operational Group had telephone links with my command in Kumbor and with my command post in Kupari. A direct, secure telephone link and also another system of radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the state of the communications system at that time? Just up to that time in general, what was the state of the communications system within the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the communications system did function between the 2nd Operational Group and the 9th Sector. There were no problems there in relation to its functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did General Strugar issue any orders to you concerning the shelling or issue any orders to anyone else to stop the shelling at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which orders he issued to his organs at the command. Actually, I don't know exactly where General Strugar was, whether he was at the command post in Trebinje or in Podgorica, but I know what he ordered me. He ordered to have the attacks stopped, and he agreed with the measures that I had taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an approximate time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was during the first telephone call when I spoke to him. And when I told him that what was underway was the sending of the chief of staff to the observation post of Captain Kovacevic and that I would send Colonel Kovacevic, who was in charge of that unit, and I believe that the two of them will manage to resolve this situation in the fastest possible way. I informed him that I was going to Cavtat, from where the links to Dubrovnik were the best. At the same time, waiting for the helicopter that was supposed to come and fetch me so that I could go to the Golubovci airport in Podgorica in order to go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, you indicated that you had been informed by Minister Rudolf that the Old Town was being shelled. Did you issue any orders to your units to not shell the Old Town, to protect it according to all orders that mandated its protection? That morning, during that attack, did you issue orders to those units that were involved that were under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately in the morning, I conveyed to Kozaric that he should relay to the division -- or rather, the two batteries that were possibly within the range of the Old Town of Dubrovnik - this is the 130-millimetre battery and the 85-millimetre battery - that he should prohibit them from using any of this and to tell Captain Kovacevic that he is not going to get any artillery by way of support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you specifically issue an order that said: Do not shell the Old Town, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. What I'm saying is not a dialogue that I'm lining up now. The basic elements of all these orders are part of the war diary. I read this after these events were over, and also in preparation for my defence. This document does exist in the archives, and I analysed it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Speaking about the morning of the 6th, are we speaking about the same date? Did you on the morning of the 6th, when this attack against the Old Town took place, did you issue, after you learned about the attack, on order not to attack the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did General Strugar issue, that morning, an order not to attack the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, in his order, in his written order, in the Decision to Order Operations, that's the name of the document, that was written on the evening of the 5th for the 6th and it is valid for the 6th, his organs wrote that what is prohibited is the opening of fire, starting from 1200 hours on the 6th of December. That is what it says quite literally in that order. As for other orders of his, I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think so. I just want to see if it might help to get one more -- I think so. I think the next line will take a little too long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I'm sorry I interrupted you. I think that it would be necessary to resolve the question of the witness's communications over the weekend, namely whether the witness is aware of fact that he cannot discuss the subject of his evidence with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would expect that he's been duly advised of his position during his briefing. But you will understand, Admiral, that over the weekend you should not discuss your evidence with anyone. And I must ask you to return again on Monday morning. Thank you. We will adjourn for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
